    About Me

    I am a physicist and PhD candidate in Condensed Matter and Nanosciences at UNAM, working in the group of Dr. Alejandro Reyes-Coronado. My research sits at the intersection of classical electrodynamics and quantum electron microscopy: I develop semi-analytical and numerical methods to describe how fast electrons exchange linear and angular momentum with nanostructures, and how those interactions show up in electron energy-loss spectra.

    Research Interests

    • Theoretical electron microscopy (STEM-EELS)
    • Multislice simulation methods
    • Nanoplasmonics and electron–matter momentum transfer
    • Vibrational and magnetic EELS (magnons)
    • High-performance scientific computing

    News

    • 2025–2026 — Research stay at Uppsala University (Materials Theory Division), collaborating with Dr. Jan Rusz on an efficient magnetic multislice implementation for predicting magnon signals in STEM-EELS.
    • 2024 — First-author paper on angular momentum transfer to non-spherical nanoparticles published in Ultramicroscopy (DOI).
    • 2023–2025 — First-author contributions presented at Microscopy & Microanalysis (M&M) and Frontiers in Optics + Laser Science (FiO), the two leading venues for this work.
    • Ongoing — Supervising an undergraduate thesis project at UNAM.

    Background

    I completed my B.S. in Physics (2019) and M.S. in Physical Sciences (2023) at UNAM, the latter on angular momentum transfer from swift electrons to large nanoparticles. My doctoral work extends this to non-spherical geometries and non-local dielectric response, using UNAM’s GRID-UNAM supercomputing resources to build efficient computational frameworks for these calculations. Expected defense: 2027.

    Through the AALD-PAEP-UNAM research visit grant, I spent time at the Materials Theory Department, Uppsala University, working with Dr. Jan Rusz’s group on a magnetic extension of the multislice method (FDES) for simulating magnon-EELS signals — a natural extension of the numerical methods developed during my momentum-transfer work into a new, closely related problem.
